title: The Anechoic Chamber and the Ramapo Mountains: Cage, the Prepared Piano, and the Room That Is Never Empty
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Only Child of an Inventor

stops.name: Good Samaritan Hospital, Los Angeles: the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested. The coordinate is the current hospital site at 616 South Witmer Street; the 1912 building footprint may differ slightly.
stops.campa: John Milton Cage Jr. is born in downtown Los Angeles, the only child of the inventor John Milton Cage Sr. and Lucretia Harvey Cage, called Crete. The father is a man who builds things that have not been built before, and the household runs on his patents and on the intervals between them. At around eighteen months, or fifteen depending on the telling, the boy swallows a quantity of strychnine tablets and is taken for emergency treatment. A newspaper of the day carries the story and every biographer since has repeated it. He survives it without apparent injury.
suggested_refs: The patent record of John Milton Cage Sr., Los Angeles inventor
sources: Newspaper report of the strychnine episode as relayed by later biographers (tagged R: not independently confirmed against the original)

stops.name: Hollywood Bowl, Los Angeles: the speech for a day of quiet
stops.date_confidence: The year is attested; the month and day of the oratorical contest are not fixed by the sources reached, and the date defaults to January by this file's convention. The later reading of the speech as a prophecy of 4'33" is retrospective interpretation and is tagged R.
stops.campa: A sixteen-year-old wins a Southern California oratorical contest and delivers the winning speech at the Hollywood Bowl. His proposal is that the United States should keep one day of national quiet, so that Americans might stop talking long enough to hear what other people were thinking. It is an argument about diplomacy made by a boy who has taken piano lessons and nothing more. Writers who come to him after 1952 read the speech backward as a first draft of the silent piece. What the boy at the microphone thought he was proposing, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: The prize-winning oratorical text of 1928, cited in the standard biographies

stops.name: Los Angeles High School: the valedictorian
stops.date_confidence: The year is attested; June is inferred from the ordinary graduation calendar. The coordinate corrects the research pool's 34.0538, -118.3229 to the school's Olympic Boulevard campus, occupied since 1917.
stops.campa: He graduates first in his class from the school on Olympic Boulevard. The grades come easily and the coursework does not hold him; what holds him is the piano, which he has been playing since childhood without any thought of doing it professionally. Music at this point is what his hands do while the rest of him decides on a career. The family expectation runs toward the ministry or toward writing, and he shares it. He is fifteen through most of his final year and sixteen by the time he collects the diploma.
suggested_refs: Los Angeles High School yearbook and commencement records, class of 1928

stops.name: Pomona College, Claremont: the shelf everyone is sent to
stops.date_confidence: Enrollment in 1928 and departure in 1930 are attested; September is inferred from the academic calendar. The coordinate corrects the pool's 34.0967, -117.7198, which sits about six hundred metres southwest of the campus.
stops.campa: He enters Pomona meaning to read theology and write, and leaves after two years having concluded that the institution manufactures likeness: a class sent to one shelf for one assigned book, and graded on how nearly they agree. Duchamp and Joyce reach him here, through teachers and through reading, before the music does. He tells his parents that Europe will educate a writer better than Claremont can. They agree with him, and they pay the passage.
suggested_refs: Pomona College registrar's records, 1928-1930

stops.name: Paris: the lessons with Lazare Levy
stops.date_confidence: Cage is in Europe from 1930 into 1931; the month of his arrival in Paris is not fixed by the sources reached. The pin is the canonical Paris coordinate inherited from the corpus.
stops.campa: He sails from Galveston, lands at Le Havre, and comes to Paris with no plan in hand except to look at things. He spends a month on Gothic architecture, drops it for painting, drops that for music, and takes piano lessons with Lazare Levy. What he is acquiring is the habit of moving to whichever art has just stopped being obvious to him. He is seventeen, he has no training worth the name, and his parents in Los Angeles are paying for all eighteen months of it.
suggested_refs: Lazare Levy's teaching register at the Paris Conservatoire, 1930-1931

stops.name: Seville: the corner where everything arrives at once
stops.date_confidence: R. The episode is known only from Cage's own retelling, decades later; the sources reached carry no letter, notebook, or contemporary record of it, and the date is set to order the segment.
stops.campa: Standing at a street corner in Seville he notices that more is happening at once than one attention can hold, and that none of it is arranged: sounds and sights arriving together and belonging to nothing in particular. He tells the story for the next sixty years as the moment multiplicity stopped being a problem to be solved. No letter, notebook, or contemporary record from that autumn mentions it. The only source for the corner in Seville is Cage himself, describing it decades after the fact.
suggested_refs: Cage's autobiographical statements and lectures on the Seville corner
sources: john_cage.dossier.md (tagged R in the research pool; no independent corroboration found)

stops.name: Palma de Mallorca: the mathematical scores, thrown out
stops.date_confidence: The Mallorca composing is placed in the 1930-1931 European stay; the month is not fixed by the sources reached and defaults to January.
stops.campa: On Mallorca he begins to compose, and he does it by system: pieces generated from mathematical procedures rather than from taste. He works this way for some months, plays the results, and destroys them, because what the systems produce does not sound like anything he wants to hear. Twenty years later the same instinct will return with the second half amputated, when he stops asking whether he wants to hear it. He is eighteen and has finished nothing he is willing to keep.
suggested_refs: Cage's account of the abandoned Mallorca systems in his autobiographical lectures

stops.name: Santa Monica: lecturing on what he read last week
stops.date_confidence: The return from Europe is dated 1931 and the Santa Monica period runs to about 1933; the month is not fixed by the sources reached.
stops.campa: Back in California without a degree and without money, he settles in Santa Monica and supports himself lecturing on modern art and modern music to whoever will pay, staying about a week ahead of his audience by reading in the library. Nothing in the arrangement resembles a career. The collector Galka Scheyer opens the progressive art circles of Southern California to him. He begins composition lessons with the pianist Richard Buhlig in Los Angeles, and the lecture fees pay for them.
suggested_refs: The Galka Scheyer collection and its Southern California circle, 1931-1933

stops.name: The New School, New York: Cowell, Weiss, and the YWCA walls
stops.date_confidence: 1933 is attested for the New York study with Henry Cowell and Adolph Weiss; the month is inferred. The coordinate is the New School's Manhattan campus, a known Cowell teaching base in the period, not a confirmed lesson venue. The Brooklyn wall-washing work is tagged R.
stops.campa: Buhlig sends him east. He studies with Adolph Weiss and sits in Henry Cowell's classes at the New School, where the syllabus includes the music of Asia and Africa and where Cowell demonstrates his own practice of reaching past the keyboard to play the piano's strings directly by hand. Cage has no money and takes work washing walls at a Brooklyn YWCA, composing in the hours around it. The instrument he will invent in Seattle in seven years is lying open in front of him here, lid up, strings exposed.
suggested_refs: Henry Cowell's string-piano works and his New School teaching syllabus, 1933-1934

stops.name: University of Southern California, Los Angeles: the promise and the wall
stops.date_confidence: The research pool's '1934/1935' compresses two institutions. Schoenberg does not reach Los Angeles until autumn 1934; the defensible sequence is private lessons from 1934, classwork at USC in 1935-36, then UCLA from 1936. The stop is dated 1935 at the USC campus and the exchange about the wall survives only in Cage's own retelling, tagged R.
stops.campa: Schoenberg, newly arrived from Europe, asks whether the young man will devote his life to music. Cage says he will. Schoenberg then says there will be no fee, and teaches him for two years, in class and privately, at USC and then at UCLA. The verdict on harmony is delivered early and without softening: Cage has no feeling for it, and harmony will be a wall he can never pass through. What Cage says back, in the version he tells a quarter of a century later, is that he will spend his life beating his head against that wall.
stops.quote: In that case I will devote my life to beating my head against that wall.
stops.quote_source: Cage recounting his reply to Arnold Schoenberg, in the lecture 'Indeterminacy' (1958)
suggested_refs: Schoenberg's Los Angeles teaching rosters, USC 1935-36 and UCLA from 1936

stops.name: Yuma County Courthouse, Yuma: the marriage to Xenia Kashevaroff
stops.date_confidence: The date is attested; the courthouse coordinate is tagged R in the research pool, the exact venue not confirmed.
stops.campa: He marries Xenia Andreyevna Kashevaroff, born in Alaska, an artist and a bookbinder, at Yuma on the Arizona line. Over the next seven years they move five times, Los Angeles to San Francisco to Seattle to Chicago to New York, hauling the brake drums and tin cans and gongs of his percussion orchestra from one borrowed room to the next. She plays in the front rank of the ensembles for the whole decade. The marriage lasts ten years and the accounts of that decade barely mention her.
suggested_refs: Yuma County marriage register, 7 June 1935

stops.name: UCLA, Los Angeles: the man at the instrument while others move
stops.date_confidence: The UCLA accompanying work is dated 1936-1938; September is inferred from the academic calendar.
stops.campa: He takes work at UCLA playing for dance classes and teaches, with his aunt Phoebe Harvey James, a course in musical accompaniment for rhythmic expression. The job decides the shape of the next fifty-four years, though nothing about it looks decisive at the time: he is the man at the instrument while other people move, and every major thing he makes will be made in that position or in argument with it. A dance floor wants percussion, and percussion is what he starts to write.
suggested_refs: UCLA dance department course listings, 1936-1938

segments.name: Brake Drums and the Prepared Piano

stops.name: Mills College, Oakland: north on Cowell's advice
stops.date_confidence: 1938 is attested; the month is inferred. The pin is inherited from the corpus entry for the Mills College campus; the geography pass proposed 37.7783, -122.1811 for the same campus, and the discrepancy is recorded in the report rather than resolved here.
stops.campa: On Cowell's advice he moves to the Bay Area, teaches at Mills College, and writes for the choreographer Marian van Tuyl. In San Francisco he meets Lou Harrison, who is doing precisely what he is doing, building percussion orchestras out of what a hardware store sells, and the two of them programme each other's music for years afterward. It is the first audience he has had that does not need to be argued into accepting a car brake drum as an instrument.
suggested_refs: The Cage-Harrison percussion repertory of the late 1930s; Double Music (1941)

stops.name: Cornish School, Seattle: the accompanist and the dance student
stops.date_confidence: Cage is at Cornish from 1938 to 1941; the sources disagree on whether he and Merce Cunningham first met in 1938 or 1939. The pin is inherited byte for byte from merce_cunningham.journey.json.
stops.campa: He comes to Seattle to accompany Bonnie Bird's dance classes at the Cornish School and stays three years. He builds a percussion orchestra out of brake drums, tin cans, gongs, and whatever else rings when struck, and puts on concerts of it in a city that has not asked for any. Among Bird's students is a nineteen-year-old from a Washington lumber town who came for theatre and is turning into a dancer. The partnership that begins in this building will run fifty-four years, to the day Cage dies. Merce Cunningham leaves for New York and Martha Graham the following year.
suggested_refs: Cornish School enrollment and faculty records, 1937-1941
sources: merce_cunningham.journey.json, stop 'Seattle, the accompanist at the piano'

stops.name: Cornish School, Seattle: the bolts between the strings
stops.date_confidence: 1940 is attested for the invention and for Bacchanale; the sources reached do not fix the month, so the date defaults to January. Pin inherited from merce_cunningham.journey.json.
stops.campa: Syvilla Fort asks him for music for a dance called Bacchanale. There is no room in the theatre for a percussion orchestra and there is a piano on the stage. He tries to write a percussive piano piece and it will not come, so he opens the lid and puts objects between the strings: screws, bolts, a strip of rubber, a coin. Each one detunes and dampens a single note into something with no name in the vocabulary. One player at one instrument now commands an orchestra of timbres nobody has classified, and the next decade of his music will come out of the gap between two strings. Bacchanale is written on the altered piano, and Fort dances to it.
suggested_refs: The preparation tables of Bacchanale (1940) and of the later prepared-piano works

stops.name: Chicago School of Design: the year at the New Bauhaus
stops.date_confidence: The Chicago period is dated 1941-1942; September is inferred from the academic calendar.
stops.campa: He teaches at the Chicago School of Design, the transplanted Bauhaus, and organizes percussion activity at the University of Chicago. The students there have been taught that a material is whatever can be done with it. He has been practising that doctrine for years without having a name for it. Xenia works and the ensembles grow. At the end of the year the Cages count what they have, judge that Chicago will not hold them, and go east with almost nothing in hand.
suggested_refs: Chicago School of Design course records under Moholy-Nagy, 1941-1942

segments.name: New York, and the Instruction from the East

stops.name: New York: the house of Peggy Guggenheim and Max Ernst
stops.date_confidence: The 1942 arrival is attested; the month is not. The coordinate is an approximate placeholder for Guggenheim's East Side house, the exact address not confirmed by the sources reached, and the collapse of the gallery concert is tagged R.
stops.campa: The Cages reach New York from Chicago with almost no money and are taken in by Peggy Guggenheim and Max Ernst. A concert is arranged to open Guggenheim's gallery. Then the Museum of Modern Art offers him a percussion programme of his own and he accepts it, and the gallery concert, the shipping of his instruments, and the hospitality all evaporate together. He is thirty, known in New York, and has nowhere to live. The museum concert goes ahead in February 1943, to a full house and a photograph in the press.
suggested_refs: The Museum of Modern Art percussion concert of February 1943 and its press coverage

stops.name: New York: the first solo concert, Cage at the piano
stops.date_confidence: April 1944 is attested. The pin is the canonical New York coordinate inherited from merce_cunningham.journey.json.
stops.campa: Cunningham gives the first concert of his own choreography, six solos, and Cage writes the music and plays it. Neither of them has a company, a theatre, or a public. What they have is a procedure: dance and music made separately, to the same lengths of time, brought together only on the night, so that neither illustrates the other and neither is subordinate to it. This evening is the first time the procedure is done in front of anyone. They will keep it for half a century without amending it.
stops.quote: John Cage and I became interested in the use of chance in the 50's.
stops.quote_source: Merce Cunningham, speaking in Merce Cunningham: A Lifetime of Dance (dir. Charles Atlas, 2000)
suggested_refs: Programme of Cunningham's first solo concert, New York, April 1944
sources: merce_cunningham.journey.json, stop 'New York, the first solo concert with Cage at the piano'

stops.name: 326 Monroe Street, New York: the divorce and the exchange with Gita Sarabhai
stops.date_confidence: The Monroe Street tenancy is tagged R and runs from about 1946 to 1954. The divorce from Xenia Kashevaroff is dated 1945 and Sarabhai's lessons 1946; the stop takes 1946 to order the segment. Sarabhai's teaching is confirmed only against standard biography, not refetched.
stops.campa: The marriage ends. He takes rooms on the Lower East Side with the river in the window, and a young Indian musician, Gita Sarabhai, arrives wanting lessons in Western counterpoint and proposing an exchange: she will teach him Indian music and the philosophy attached to it, hour for hour. Everything he writes afterwards is written under what he carries out of those hours: a use for music that has nothing to do with expressing the man who wrote it, and a purpose for art imported wholesale from outside Europe, that art imitates nature in her manner of operation.
suggested_refs: Ananda Coomaraswamy, The Transformation of Nature in Art, the source of the formula Cage took from Sarabhai's circle
sources: Kenneth Silverman, Begin Again (secondary confirmation only; not refetched)

stops.name: Black Mountain College: the summer of the Baron Medusa
stops.date_confidence: Summer 1948 is attested; July is given to order the segment. The pin is inherited byte for byte from merce_cunningham.journey.json and buckminster_fuller.journey.json.
stops.campa: He and Cunningham spend the summer teaching in the North Carolina mountains, and he stages Erik Satie's Le Piege de Meduse, a play with music that has never been performed in America. Buckminster Fuller plays the Baron; Cunningham is the mechanical monkey. Cage is thirty-five and has decided that Satie, not Beethoven, is the composer American music should have been following, and he spends the summer arguing it. Josef Albers is on the faculty that season, and Anni Albers, and Willem de Kooning.
suggested_refs: Cage's Black Mountain lecture in defense of Satie, summer 1948
sources: merce_cunningham.journey.json, stop 'Black Mountain College, the summer of the Baron Medusa'

stops.name: Carnegie Hall, New York: Sonatas and Interludes
stops.date_confidence: The Ajemian recital is dated 1949 and the composition of the cycle to 1946-1948; the sources reached do not fix the month of the recital, and the date defaults to January.
stops.campa: Maro Ajemian, to whom the cycle is dedicated, plays the sixteen sonatas and four interludes at Carnegie Hall on a piano loaded with screws, bolts, rubber, and plastic, each object set at a measured distance along its string. It runs a little over an hour and it is organized on Indian aesthetics: the eight permanent emotions, four light and four dark, and their common tendency toward tranquillity. For one season it makes him a famous American composer, plainly and without qualification, and he is never that again.
suggested_refs: The preparation table of Sonatas and Interludes (1946-1948)

stops.name: Paris: the Guggenheim year and Pierre Boulez
stops.date_confidence: The fellowship and the European travel are dated 1949; the month in Paris is not fixed by the sources reached. The pin is the canonical Paris coordinate inherited from the corpus.
stops.campa: A Guggenheim Fellowship and an award from the National Institute of Arts and Letters pay for six months in Europe. In Paris he finds Pierre Boulez, twenty-four, and they talk and then correspond for years, each treating the other as the only serious composer of his generation on the far side of the ocean. Boulez is building total control over every parameter. Cage is walking toward the coin toss. The friendship survives until the method does, and no longer.
stops.quote: adoption of a philosophy tinged with Orientalism that masks a basic weakness in compositional technique.
stops.quote_source: Pierre Boulez on Cage, quoted with citation on the Wikipedia article 'John Cage'
suggested_refs: The Cage-Boulez correspondence, 1949-1954, published in edited form
sources: john_cage.dossier.md (no pierre_boulez journey file exists in the corpus)

stops.name: Carnegie Hall, New York: leaving before the Rachmaninoff
stops.date_confidence: January 1950 is attested for the meeting with Morton Feldman; the day is not fixed by the sources reached.
stops.campa: At a New York Philharmonic concert two men stay through the Webern and then walk out rather than sit for the Rachmaninoff that follows it, and they meet each other in the lobby doing exactly that. Morton Feldman is twenty-four. Out of the lobby comes the loose circle later labelled the New York School: Feldman, Christian Wolff, Earle Brown, and the pianist David Tudor, who will give the first performance of nearly everything Cage writes for the next twenty years.
suggested_refs: The New York Philharmonic programme for January 1950

stops.name: Columbia University, New York: the Suzuki lectures
stops.date_confidence: R throughout. The research pool places Cage at D. T. Suzuki's Columbia lectures around 1950, and no fetched primary source confirms either his attendance or the dates; Cage's own accounts of how long he attended are inconsistent. The pin is the Columbia coordinate used elsewhere in the corpus.
stops.campa: He sits in on Daisetz Suzuki's lectures on Zen at Columbia. What he carries out of the room is a licence: that a composer's preferences are the obstacle rather than the material, that sounds are to be let be themselves instead of made into vehicles for a man's feelings, that purposelessness and meaninglessness are different words. He never once describes himself as a Buddhist. Everything he does after 1951 is done holding that licence. How many years he sat there, two or three, his own tellings do not agree.
stops.quote: a purposeless play which is an affirmation of life, not an attempt to bring order out of chaos nor to suggest improvements in creation, but simply a way of waking up to the very life we're living
stops.quote_source: 'Experimental Music' (1957), in Silence: Lectures and Writings (1961)
suggested_refs: D. T. Suzuki's Columbia University lecture series, 1950-1957
sources: john_cage.dossier.md (tagged R in the research pool; no fetched source confirms attendance)

stops.name: New York: the I Ching and Music of Changes
stops.date_confidence: 1951 is attested both for Wolff's gift of the I Ching and for the composition of Music of Changes; the months are not fixed. Canonical New York pin inherited from the corpus.
stops.campa: Christian Wolff brings him the newly translated I Ching, two volumes of it. Cage reads the tables of hexagrams and recognizes a machine for producing decisions that are not his own. He builds charts of sounds, durations, dynamics, and superimpositions, throws three coins for every value in the piece, and assembles Music of Changes for David Tudor out of the results. The composer's job, from here on, is to ask the questions and write down what comes back. It takes months of tossing, three coins at a time, one value at a time.
stops.quote: I can't understand why people are frightened of new ideas. I'm frightened of the old ones.
stops.quote_source: Conversing with Cage, ed. Richard Kostelanetz (1988)
suggested_refs: The Wilhelm-Baynes I Ching (Bollingen, 1950), the edition Wolff gave him
Cunningham's independently chance-derived Suite by Chance, Urbana, 24 March 1953
sources: merce_cunningham.journey.json, stop 'Urbana, Illinois, Suite by Chance'

stops.name: Harvard University, Cambridge: the anechoic chamber
stops.date_confidence: The visit is dated 1951 and rests on Cage's own repeated testimony; the month is not fixed. The engineer's identification of the two sounds as nervous system and circulation is disputed on physiological grounds, tinnitus being the usual alternative, and is tagged R.
stops.campa: He goes into the anechoic chamber at Harvard expecting silence, which is what the room exists to manufacture, and hears two sounds instead, one high and one low. The engineer on duty tells him the high one is his nervous system in operation and the low one is his blood in circulation. What he takes out of the room is not in dispute: silence, as a condition, does not occur. Whether that is what he heard, and whether a man can hear either sound at all, has been argued ever since.
stops.quote: Until I die there will be sounds. And they will continue following my death.
stops.quote_source: 'Experimental Music' (1957), in Silence: Lectures and Writings (1961)
suggested_refs: The Harvard anechoic chamber and the physiological debate over Cage's two sounds

stops.name: Black Mountain College: the untitled event
stops.date_confidence: Summer 1952 is attested; August is given to order the segment. No score survives, the surviving accounts of the running order contradict each other, and the label 'first Happening' is a later attribution by others and is tagged R.
stops.campa: In the dining hall he assigns each performer a bracket of time and lets them fill it however they wish. He reads a lecture from a stepladder; Cunningham dances through an audience seated facing four ways; David Tudor plays; Charles Olson and M. C. Richards read poetry; Robert Rauschenberg runs records on a wind-up phonograph with his white paintings hung overhead. Nothing is coordinated except the clock. Afterwards nobody can agree on the order of events, and the accounts written down years later contradict one another on nearly every point.
suggested_refs: Allan Kaprow's later coinage of the term Happening and its retrospective application to this evening

stops.name: Maverick Concert Hall, near Woodstock: four minutes thirty-three seconds
stops.date_confidence: The date is attested. The coordinate corrects the research pool to the figure given for Maverick Concert Hall, which stands off Maverick Road in Hurley, Ulster County, though it is customarily addressed as Woodstock; two other pins for this venue circulate in the pool and the three-way discrepancy is recorded in the report.
stops.campa: David Tudor sits at the piano in a wooden hall in the woods, closes the keyboard lid, and does not play. He opens and closes it twice more to mark the movement divisions, turning pages as he goes, and after four minutes and thirty-three seconds he stands up. Wind in the trees for the first movement, rain on the roof for the second, and in the third the audience itself, talking and walking out. The piece consists of whatever is heard while it is not being played. The manuscript is later lost.
stops.quote: Wherever we are, what we hear is mostly noise. When we ignore it, it disturbs us.
stops.quote_source: 'The Future of Music: Credo' (1937), in Silence: Lectures and Writings (1961)
suggested_refs: The 2002 action by Cage's publisher against Mike Batt over 'A One Minute Silence', and Batt's 2010 statement that the reported six-figure settlement was in fact a donation of one thousand pounds

segments.name: Stony Point, the Mushrooms, and the School

stops.name: Black Mountain College: the company is formed
stops.date_confidence: Summer 1953 is attested; August is given to order the segment. Pin inherited byte for byte from merce_cunningham.journey.json.
stops.campa: In one of the college's last summers Cunningham forms a company out of the dancers on hand, and Cage is its founding musician and, for the rest of his life, its music director and its adviser on everything else. There is no money at all, and Cage will spend a substantial part of the next thirty years finding some by means that have nothing to do with composing. The founding roster: Carolyn Brown, Viola Farber, Marianne Preger-Simon, Remy Charlip, and a young Paul Taylor.
suggested_refs: The founding roster of the Merce Cunningham Dance Company, Black Mountain College, summer 1953
sources: merce_cunningham.journey.json, stop 'Black Mountain College, the company is formed'

stops.name: Gate Hill Cooperative, Stony Point: the cabin and the mushrooms
stops.date_confidence: The move is placed in the summer of 1954 and the tenancy runs into the 1960s; the coordinate for the cooperative is tagged R in the research pool.
stops.campa: Displaced from Monroe Street, he moves to an artists' cooperative in Rockland County and lives in a cabin of roughly ten feet by twenty at twenty-four dollars and fifteen cents a month, among potters, weavers, composers, and their children. He is poor enough that food is a live question and the woods around him are full of it. The knowledge he builds up in those woods is about to pay the company's bills. He learns the fungi of the region systematically, and in 1962 he helps found the New York Mycological Society.
suggested_refs: The Gate Hill Cooperative at Stony Point and its 1950s residents
The New York Mycological Society, founded 1962

stops.name: The New School, New York: the composition class
stops.date_confidence: The class runs from 1956 to 1961; September 1956 is given to order the segment.
stops.campa: For five years he teaches experimental composition at the New School to a class that is mostly not composers. Allan Kaprow is in it, and George Brecht, Dick Higgins, Al Hansen, Jackson Mac Low. He gives them chance operations, silence, and the proposition that a score may instruct anyone to do anything whatever. He teaches it as a course in music and it comes out the far end as a decade of art. Within three years Kaprow is staging Happenings and the Fluxus events are beginning.
stops.quote: Value judgments are destructive to our proper business, which is curiosity and awareness.
stops.quote_source: Conversing with Cage, ed. Richard Kostelanetz (1988)
suggested_refs: New School for Social Research course records, 1956-1961
George Brecht's event scores and the early Fluxus publications

stops.name: Milan: the mushrooms on television
stops.date_confidence: 1959 is attested for the appearances on Lascia o raddoppia?; the sources reached name Italy without naming the studio city, and Milan is used as a representative coordinate, tagged R. The month is not fixed.
stops.campa: He appears on the Italian quiz show Lascia o raddoppia? as an expert on mushrooms, week after week, answering questions on fungi in front of an audience of millions and performing a piece of his own between rounds, so that the country hears amplified water and radios and a piano full of hardware in prime time. He answers everything correctly and takes the top prize. The money goes into the Cunningham company, which buys a vehicle with it and tours a season it could not otherwise have afforded.
suggested_refs: RAI broadcast records for Lascia o raddoppia?, 1959
sources: john_cage.dossier.md, cross-referenced against David Revill, The Roaring Silence (not refetched this pass)

stops.name: Wesleyan University, Middletown: Silence
stops.date_confidence: The Wesleyan fellowship dates from 1960 and Silence is published in October 1961; the stop takes the publication date and carries both facts.
stops.campa: A fellowship at the Center for Advanced Studies gives him, at forty-eight, his first institutional home, and the university press collects twenty years of his lectures and articles into a book. The typography follows the talks rather than the essays: columns, gaps, blank measures where the page has to wait. The book goes further than the music does. Composers who never hear a note of his read it, and so do poets, painters, dancers, architects, and a large number of people who make nothing at all.
stops.quote: I have nothing to say / and I am saying it / and that is poetry / as I need it
stops.quote_source: 'Lecture on Nothing' (1949), in Silence: Lectures and Writings (Wesleyan University Press, 1961), p. 109; line breaks as printed, without terminal punctuation
suggested_refs: Silence: Lectures and Writings (Wesleyan, 1961) and its Czech, Italian, and Japanese translations

stops.name: Pocket Theatre, Third Avenue, New York: eight hundred and forty times
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Pin inherited byte for byte from erik_satie.journey.json and merce_cunningham.journey.json.
stops.campa: He organizes the first complete performance of Erik Satie's Vexations, a single page of music carrying an instruction to repeat it eight hundred and forty times. A relay of pianists takes it in turn, Cage and David Tudor and Christian Wolff and John Cale and Joshua Rifkin among them. Fifteen years after putting Buckminster Fuller into a Satie play in North Carolina, he is still making the same argument by other means. The performance runs eighteen hours and forty minutes, from the evening into the following afternoon.
suggested_refs: Satie's manuscript instruction to Vexations and the question of whether it is a performance direction at all

stops.name: Paris: the world tour crosses Europe
stops.date_confidence: The tour runs six months in 1964; June is given for the European leg. The pin is the canonical Paris coordinate inherited from the corpus.
stops.campa: The Cunningham company goes around the world for six months on money that does not exist, through Western and Eastern Europe, India, Thailand, and Japan, and Cage travels as musician, negotiator, fundraiser, and the man who talks to the presenter when the fee fails to arrive. In Paris the reception is loud in both directions and the company acquires the second city it will keep for forty years. Robert Rauschenberg is the designer on the tour and leaves the company at the end of it.

stops.name: Tokyo: the second meeting with Toru Takemitsu
stops.date_confidence: The Japanese leg of the 1964 tour is attested; the month is not fixed by the sources reached. Pin inherited from merce_cunningham.journey.json.
stops.campa: The tour reaches Japan and he sees Toru Takemitsu again. Cage has been taking from Asia since Gita Sarabhai handed him a purpose for art in 1946, and from Suzuki's lecture room after that. Japanese composers of Takemitsu's generation have been reading him for a decade and taking from the American a permission to return to their own instruments and their own silences without being called reactionary for it. Neither party can say cleanly which direction the borrowing runs.
suggested_refs: Toru Takemitsu's writings on Cage and on the return to Japanese instruments

stops.name: University of Illinois, Urbana: HPSCHD
stops.date_confidence: 1969 is attested for the premiere; the sources reached do not fix the month, and the date defaults to January. Pin inherited byte for byte from merce_cunningham.journey.json.
stops.campa: With the computer-music pioneer Lejaren Hiller he makes HPSCHD: seven amplified harpsichords, fifty-two computer-generated tapes each tuned to a different division of the octave, and thousands of slides and films thrown across every surface of an arena, running for hours while the audience walks about inside it. The I Ching operations that cost him months of coin-tossing in 1951 are run here by a mainframe in minutes. There is no seat anywhere in the arena from which the work can be heard whole.
suggested_refs: The ILLIAC computer output and the printed KNOBS sheets issued with the HPSCHD recording

stops.name: 107 Bank Street, New York: the apartment in the West Village
stops.date_confidence: The Bank Street years run from about 1971, when the company takes studios at Westbeth. The domestic arrangement is tagged R here as it is in merce_cunningham.journey.json, from which the pin is inherited byte for byte.
stops.campa: The company takes studios at Westbeth above the Hudson and Cage and Cunningham live around the corner on Bank Street. They have been together thirty-three years and have never made any public statement about it; the field knows, and the notices go on saying collaborators. The apartment holds plants, which he waters, stones, mushroom guides, chess sets, and the machines David Tudor keeps building. He cooks. He answers his post himself, all of it, and it arrives from everywhere.

stops.name: 101 West 18th Street, New York: the last loft
stops.date_confidence: R. The standard date for the move is 1979 and Cage lives here until his death, but no fetched source pins the year; the research pool carried an incorrect 'late 1960s' dating that inverted the sequence with the Bank Street years, and the correction is set out in the report. The macrobiotic diet belongs to this late period, not to 1965 as the pool first had it; the attribution to Yoko Ono's recommendation is standard biography and is tagged R.
stops.campa: The last address, a loft with plants, stones, and a long table where he writes mesostics down the spine of other men's names. Arthritis arrives, then sciatica, arteriosclerosis, and a stroke, and he goes onto a strict macrobiotic regime that stops the arthritis and, by his own reckoning, takes ten years off him. He is composing, printmaking, writing, and answering every letter that comes. He gets up before anyone else in the building and works while the street is still quiet.
stops.quote: As far as consistency of thought goes, I prefer inconsistency.
suggested_refs: The mesostic series written at West 18th Street, 1979-1992

stops.name: Cologne: Roaratorio, an Irish circus on Finnegans Wake
stops.date_confidence: 1979 is attested for the work and the commission is given as West German radio in Cologne; the sources reached do not fix a premiere date more precisely, and the date defaults to January.
stops.campa: For West German radio he makes a piece out of James Joyce's last book. A mesostic text is drawn through Finnegans Wake on Joyce's own name; Cage reads it aloud; underneath run field recordings made in the hundreds of places the novel names, with Irish traditional musicians playing across the whole of it. Nothing is synchronized with anything else. The novel is continuously audible in the result and not once legible in it, which is a fair description of reading the novel. He calls the piece Roaratorio: An Irish Circus on Finnegans Wake.
suggested_refs: The Roaratorio field-recording itinerary through the place names of Finnegans Wake

stops.name: Frankfurt: Europeras 1 and 2
stops.date_confidence: 1987 is attested for the Frankfurt premiere; the sources reached do not fix the month, and the date defaults to January by this file's convention.
stops.campa: He takes the European opera repertoire, out of copyright and lying in the public domain, and puts the whole of it through chance operations: arias, costumes, sets, lighting cues, and stage business assigned independently to singers who each perform something they already know, in a house where nothing has been rehearsed together. He is seventy-five years old and has never written an opera before. Two centuries of Europe arrive at once, with nobody appointed to sort them out.

stops.campa: He receives the Kyoto Prize in Arts and Philosophy, and at Takaragaike he gives the commemorative lecture, which he titles An Extended Autobiography. He is seventy-seven years old, and the honour arrives from the direction he has been facing since Gita Sarabhai knocked on his door in 1946. The citation credits his chance operation with becoming one of the major styles in contemporary music, and calls him a rebel against Western music and a prophet who has foretold the spirit of the coming era.
stops.quote: We need not destroy the past. It is gone.

stops.campa: On the evening of the eleventh of August he is making tea for the two of them in the loft on West 18th Street when he has a stroke. Cunningham is in the room. They take him to St. Vincent's in Greenwich Village and he dies early the next morning, seventy-nine years old, a few weeks short of the eightieth-birthday festivals being prepared for him in several countries, which are performed as memorials instead. He had been in poor health for a decade and working every day of it. Cunningham cancels nothing and dances the autumn tour.

stops.campa: He is cremated and the ashes go into the hills above the cooperative where he lived in a cabin for the price of a week's groceries and learned to name the fungi of the county. There is no grave, no stone, no plaque, and no plot number, so there is nowhere on earth a visitor can stand and be told that John Cage is here. His parents' ashes had been scattered on the same ground years before him, and he had asked, in so many words, for exactly the same. The estate, the papers, the works, and the rights all go afterwards into a trust at a college up the Hudson.

stops.name: St. Burchardi Church, Halberstadt: the chord that lasts a year
stops.date_confidence: Posthumous, and flagged as such: the performance begins on 5 September 2001, the eighty-ninth anniversary of Cage's birth, and is scheduled to end in 2640. The 639-year span was fixed by the John Cage Organ Foundation Halberstadt, not by Cage, who wrote only the instruction as slow as possible; that attribution is tagged R. The coordinate corrects two conflicting points in the research pool to the figure given for the Burchardikloster.
stops.campa: In a deconsecrated church in Saxony-Anhalt an organ built for the purpose begins a performance of Organ2/ASLSP scheduled to run six hundred and thirty-nine years. The opening seventeen months are a rest. Sandbags hold the keys down between changes; the changes fall on the fifth of a month, sometimes a year apart, sometimes longer, and people travel there to be present while one note replaces another. Cage supplied four words, as slow as possible. The six hundred and thirty-nine years were fixed by a foundation in Halberstadt, nine years after he died.
